title: Judges 13:8–20
context: Manoah prays for the messenger to return and teach them how to raise the child. The angel appears again, repeats the instructions, declines food, and directs any offering to the LORD. When Manoah asks his name, the angel replies that it is “incomprehensible” (footnoted in the WEB as ‘wonderful’), and he ascends in the altar’s flame. The scene parallels Gideon’s encounter in Judges 6. Both traditions read it as shared ground about prayer, hospitality, worship, and reverence, while leaving the messenger’s identity open.

verses.text: Then Manoah entreated the LORD, and said, “Oh, Lord, please let the man of God whom you sent come again to us, and teach us what we should do to the child who shall be born.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Manoah prays for the man of God to return and teach them how to raise the child. His request is humble and practical.

Arminian readers see a father seeking God’s guidance responsibly. Prayer here is a genuine request that God answers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Manoah asks for instruction rather than proof. He wants to do right by the child.

Reformed readers see godly parenting depending on God’s word. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about seeking God’s direction in raising children.

verses.text: God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman as she sat in the field; but Manoah, her husband, wasn’t with her.
verses.arminianNotes:
God listens to Manoah, and the angel returns, but again to the woman in the field while Manoah is absent. God answers, though not exactly as Manoah might have expected.

Arminian readers see God responding to prayer while keeping his own way.
verses.reformedNotes:
God hears and answers Manoah’s prayer. Yet the messenger again appears first to the wife.

Reformed readers see God answering prayer according to his wisdom. Both traditions share this reading and note that the woman continues to be honored in the story.

verses.text: The woman hurried and ran, and told her husband, saying to him, “Behold, the man who came to me that day has appeared to me.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The woman runs to tell her husband that the man has appeared again. She acts quickly.

Arminian readers see a partnership in faith between husband and wife. She brings him into the encounter.
verses.reformedNotes:
Her haste shows eagerness and trust. She does not keep the meeting to herself.

Reformed readers see the couple sharing God’s word together. Both traditions read this as shared ground about faithful communication within a household that is receiving a calling from God.

verses.text: Manoah arose and followed his wife, and came to the man, and said to him, “Are you the man who spoke to my wife?” He said, “I am.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Manoah follows his wife and asks the man whether he spoke to her; he answers, “I am.” The meeting is confirmed.

Arminian readers see Manoah’s desire to hear for himself. God allows him to share the encounter.
verses.reformedNotes:
The man confirms his identity simply. The scene moves toward Manoah’s questions.

Reformed readers see God condescending to meet his people’s needs. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without drawing more from the brief reply ‘I am’ than the narrative context supports.

verses.text: Manoah said, “Now let your words happen. What shall the child’s way of life and mission be?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Manoah asks what the child’s way of life and mission will be. He wants to understand the calling.

Arminian readers see a parent seeking to cooperate with God’s purpose for his son.
verses.reformedNotes:
Manoah asks about both the child’s manner of life and his work. The question is sincere.

Reformed readers see a father desiring to align his family with God’s plan. Both traditions share this reading and note that the messenger’s answer focuses on what has already been said.

verses.text: The LORD’s angel said to Manoah, “Of all that I said to the woman let her beware.
verses.arminianNotes:
The angel tells Manoah that the woman must observe everything he told her. The instructions do not change.

Arminian readers see that God’s word, once given, is sufficient. Faithfulness means keeping it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The angel repeats rather than adds. The original message stands.

Reformed readers see the sufficiency of God’s revealed word. Both traditions read this as shared ground: Manoah does not need new information so much as faithful obedience to what God has already said.

verses.text: She may not eat of anything that comes of the vine, neither let her drink wine or strong drink, nor eat any unclean thing. Let her observe all that I commanded her.”
verses.arminianNotes:
She must eat nothing from the vine, drink no wine or strong drink, eat nothing unclean, and observe all he commanded. The Nazirite rules are restated.

Arminian readers see clear, practical guidance for consecrated living.
verses.reformedNotes:
The restrictions echo Numbers 6:3–4, which forbids all products of the vine. The mother’s obedience supports the child’s calling.

Reformed readers see God’s word shaping the life of a family. Both traditions describe this constructively as shared ground about holiness and devotion.

verses.text: Manoah said to the LORD’s angel, “Please stay with us, that we may make a young goat ready for you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Manoah asks the angel to stay so that they can prepare a young goat for him. He offers hospitality.

Arminian readers see a generous response reminiscent of Abraham’s hospitality in Genesis 18.
verses.reformedNotes:
Manoah treats the visitor as an honored guest. He still does not know who he is.

Reformed readers see sincere kindness offered before full understanding. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note the parallel with other visitation stories in Genesis and Judges 6.

verses.text: The LORD’s angel said to Manoah, “Though you detain me, I won’t eat your bread. If you will prepare a burnt offering, you must offer it to the LORD.” For Manoah didn’t know that he was the LORD’s angel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The angel will not eat but says that any burnt offering must be offered to the LORD. Manoah still does not know he is the LORD’s angel.

Arminian readers see the messenger redirecting honor to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The visitor declines food and points to worship of the LORD. The narrator explains Manoah’s ignorance.

Reformed readers see worship rightly directed to God alone. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and both note that it does not settle the messenger’s identity.

verses.text: Manoah said to the LORD’s angel, “What is your name, that when your words happen, we may honor you?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Manoah asks the angel’s name so that they may honor him when his words come true. He wants to give proper credit.

Arminian readers see sincere gratitude and a desire to respond rightly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Manoah seeks the name in order to honor the messenger. Names in Scripture often express identity and character.

Reformed readers see a reasonable request that the visitor will turn aside. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, preparing for the reply in verse 18.

verses.text: The LORD’s angel said to him, “Why do you ask about my name, since it is incomprehensible?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The angel asks why Manoah wants his name, since it is “incomprehensible.” The WEB footnotes an alternative rendering: ‘wonderful.’

Arminian readers see a reply that guards the mystery of God’s messenger. Some connect the word with ‘Wonderful’ in Isaiah 9:6, which uses a related Hebrew term.
verses.reformedNotes:
The name is beyond Manoah’s grasp. The reply invites reverence rather than curiosity.

Reformed readers likewise note the possible connection with Isaiah 9:6 without pressing it. Both traditions treat the verse plainly and leave the messenger’s identity open, as the text does.

verses.text: So Manoah took the young goat with the meal offering, and offered it on the rock to the LORD. Then the angel did an amazing thing as Manoah and his wife watched.
verses.arminianNotes:
Manoah offers the goat and meal offering on the rock to the LORD, and the angel does something wonderful while they watch. The scene builds toward its climax.

Arminian readers see worship offered in response to God’s promise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Manoah follows the instruction of verse 16 and offers to the LORD. The narrator signals that something extraordinary follows.

Reformed readers see God accepting worship offered in faith. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with the wonder described in verse 20.

verses.text: For when the flame went up toward the sky from off the altar, the LORD’s angel ascended in the flame of the altar. Manoah and his wife watched; and they fell on their faces to the ground.
verses.arminianNotes:
As the flame rises, the LORD’s angel ascends in the flame from the altar, and Manoah and his wife fall on their faces. The encounter ends in awe.

Arminian readers see reverent worship as the fitting response to God’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes:
The ascent in the flame reveals the visitor’s heavenly origin. The couple responds with worship.

Reformed readers see God’s holiness inspiring fear and reverence. Both traditions share this reading, and both note a similar scene with Gideon in Judges 6:21–22.
